sources.locator: Learn Java; accessed 2026-07; Exceptions and Java I/O learning paths; atomic topic: Resource management and serialization boundaries
sources.claim: Try-with-resources closes each declared AutoCloseable in reverse order even when the body fails, and explicit interoperable data formats are safer boundaries than native object deserialization.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Files, sockets and database connections hold **operating-system resources** that must be **closed**. The garbage collector does **not** close them promptly, so a program that forgets can run out of file handles. **Try-with-resources** fixes this: every `AutoCloseable` declared in `try (...)` is closed automatically when the block ends, whether normally or by an **exception**, in **reverse order** of declaration. If closing also fails, that error is attached as a **suppressed** exception instead of hiding the original. At data boundaries, prefer **explicit formats** (JSON, CSV, text) over Java's built-in **object serialization**, which is fragile across versions and dangerous to load from untrusted sources.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner opens a BufferedReader, parses lines, and calls close() at the end. When one line is malformed, parsing throws, close() never runs, and after a few thousand requests the server fails with "Too many open files". A BufferedReader and underlying stream are declared in try-with-resources so cleanup occurs on normal return and on parsing failure. In this lesson you'll implement a failure-safe resource workflow and explain its cleanup behavior.

examples.title: A reader closed even when parsing fails
examples.situation: A BufferedReader and underlying stream are declared in try-with-resources so cleanup occurs on normal return and on parsing failure.
walkthrough: **A BufferedReader and underlying stream are declared in try-with-resources:** both appear in try (...).
**So cleanup occurs on normal return:** parse("42") prints close reader then close file.
**And on parsing failure:** parse("oops") will still close both before the catch runs.
examples.result: No handles leak, however often parsing fails.

examples.title: Too many open files
examples.situation: A server calls reader.close() at the end of a method, and after many malformed requests it runs out of file handles.
walkthrough: Test by forcing a parse failure and checking close ran.
examples.result: Handles are released on every path.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Garbage collection promptly closes files and sockets, so explicit resource management only improves style.
misconceptions.correction: The garbage collector frees memory, not handles, and may run much later or never. Close resources deterministically with try-with-resources.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Too many open files", why did handles run out?

analogy.example: Try-with-resources is like **a library that checks books back in automatically when you leave**, whichever exit you use, even the fire exit. Books borrowed last go back first. Waiting for the garbage collector is like **hoping someone eventually notices the overdue books**.
usefulFor: remembering auto check-in at every exit
limitations: Suppressed exceptions are notes about problems during check-in.
Deserializing untrusted data is accepting a sealed box from a stranger.

steps.explanation: Cleanup occurs on normal return, in reverse order.
Cleanup also occurs on parsing failure before the exception leaves.
The caller handles the error with no leaked resource.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing try-with-resources. Step 1, Normal return: closed is reader, then file; result is 42. Cleanup occurs on normal return, in reverse order. Step 2, Failure: exception is NumberFormatException; closed is reader, then file. Cleanup also occurs on parsing failure before the exception leaves. Step 3, Handle: printed is bad input. The caller handles the error with no leaked resource.

farTransfer.prompt: Replace a class that saves objects with ObjectOutputStream by a CSV or JSON-like text format. Validate on load, keep try-with-resources for all streams, and test round trips and malformed input.

remediation.explanation: Whenever you create something with a close() method, **declare it in try (...)**. At boundaries, ask: **is this an explicit, validated format?**
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "Too many open files".

recap.summary: To implement a failure-safe resource workflow and explain its cleanup behavior, declare every AutoCloseable in try-with-resources so it closes in reverse order on normal return and on failure, read suppressed exceptions when close also fails, and use explicit validated data formats instead of native deserialization.
